claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a stable fcc matrix.
The starting alloy exhibits high strength and fatigue performance.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by competition between a protective Al/Cr-rich oxide scale and detrimental internal oxidation of Ti.
In oxidizing atmospheres, Al and Cr selectively oxidize to form a coherent, adherent surface scale.
The Al/Cr-rich surface scale limits further degradation.
Oxidizing exposure partially segregates Ti toward the alloy interior.
Ti may undergo minor internal oxidation during oxidizing exposure.
Formation of the protective scale preserves the mechanical integrity of the fcc matrix.
A reducing atmosphere prevents formation of a stable protective oxide scale.
The absence of a robust protective scale under reducing conditions permits more aggressive and uneven internal oxidation, especially of Ti.
Internal oxidation under reducing conditions produces microstructural inhomogeneity and microcracking.
Microcracking caused by reducing exposure eventually leads to embrittlement and degraded performance.
The overall fcc phase remains intact during the proposed degradation process.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a relatively uniform, adherent Al/Cr-rich oxide layer.
Reducing exposure will produce more internal Ti oxidation and a higher microcrack density than oxidizing exposure.
Reducing exposure will diminish fatigue performance relative to the as-manufactured baseline.
The proposed oxidation mechanisms become significant above approximately 800 °C.
Oxidation is minimal below approximately 800 °C.
The controlled comparison uses air containing about 21% O2 and a low-oxygen reducing gas containing about 5% H2 at 850 °C and 950 °C.
Similar scale characteristics, internal oxidation, and mechanical degradation in both atmospheres would falsify the proposed environment-dependent mechanism.
